subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: I noticed it in Class Nine. Our English teacher would say "Beautiful!" the second anyone spoke with an accent like a news anchor. When Tanuja read her Marathi poem for the school festival, he said, "Lovely. Now, could someone read it in proper English?" Tanuja sat down and hardly spoke in class for a week. She scores higher than me in maths, and she understands that poem better than any of us. I realised I had also been giving more attention to people who used big English words. So I did something small: I asked her, in front of everyone, to explain the poem, in Marathi first, and then we translated it together. The class went quiet. She lit up. I don't think English is bad. I think fluent English gets mistaken for being smart. Tarun

qa.q: What did the English teacher say after Tanuja read her Marathi poem?
qa.a: The teacher said, "Lovely. Now, could someone read it in proper English?"

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when Tarun realised the bias?
qa.a: Tarun felt uncomfortable and a bit guilty, since Tarun had also been giving more attention to people who used big English words.

qa.q: Which choice by Tarun challenged the bias?
qa.a: Tarun asked Tanuja, in front of everyone, to explain the poem in Marathi first and then translate it together, showing that language is not intelligence.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt when she was asked to explain her poem?
qa.a: Probably proud and relieved. She lit up after a week of hardly speaking, since her own language was finally treated as worth hearing.

grounding: A teenager notices that fluent English earns respect while a regional language is treated as lesser, and resists that bias.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: I sit behind Yusuf in class, so I saw it happen twice in one week. Yusuf answers science questions in English mixed with Malayalam, and the teacher would sigh, "Speak properly, Yusuf." But when Neha gave the same answer in smooth English on Thursday, the teacher smiled and said, "Excellent." Yusuf stopped raising his hand. On Friday I stayed back and asked him to explain the experiment to me in whatever language he liked. He did, in Malayalam, and it was clearer than the textbook. I can't say how he felt about the teacher. But I've stopped copying people who sound English-y in order to sound clever. Yusuf is the smartest person I sit near. Sangeeta

qa.q: What did the teacher say to Yusuf when he mixed languages?
qa.a: The teacher would sigh, "Speak properly, Yusuf."

qa.q: What has changed in Sangeeta's thinking by the end?
qa.a: Sangeeta admires Yusuf and feels a change of heart, and has stopped copying people who sound English-y in order to sound clever.

qa.q: Which choice by Sangeeta helped Yusuf on Friday?
qa.a: Sangeeta stayed back and asked him to explain the experiment in whatever language he liked, and listened to the clear explanation in Malayalam.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt when the teacher praised the same answer from Neha?
qa.a: Probably hurt and discouraged, since he stopped raising his hand after that.

grounding: A teenager sees fluent English praised while a regional language is treated as lesser, and starts to resist that bias in themselves and others.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
Monday. In Bhavna's Class 10, the new teacher praised Sonali three times for her "beautiful English." When Ganesh answered a history question in Marathi-flavoured English, the teacher said, "Try again, properly." Ganesh's answer had been right. Bhavna noticed, and felt uneasy.
Wednesday. At lunch, Sonali imitated Ganesh's accent. Bhavna laughed along before she could stop herself. Then she saw Ganesh's face and felt her stomach drop.
Friday. In the group project, Ganesh explained the whole Maratha chapter to them in Marathi, fast and brilliant, better than any of them. Bhavna said, "Ganesh, you should present this part. In English or Marathi, whichever." Sonali rolled her eyes. Ganesh looked surprised, then nodded.
Walking home, Bhavna thought: speaking English well had never meant knowing more. She was annoyed that she'd believed it.

qa.q: How many times did the new teacher praise Sonali?
qa.a: The teacher praised Sonali three times for her "beautiful English."

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she saw Ganesh's face at lunch?
qa.a: Bhavna felt guilty and ashamed, her stomach dropping, after laughing along at the imitation.

qa.q: Which choice did Bhavna make on Friday, and why was it fair?
qa.a: She asked Ganesh to present the part he knew best in whichever language he liked, valuing his knowledge over his accent.

qa.q: How might Ganesh feel when the teacher says "Try again, properly"?
qa.a: Ganesh probably felt humiliated and discouraged, since his answer was right but was treated as lesser because of his English.

grounding: Over one week, a teenager notices fluent English being treated as a sign of intelligence and begins to resist that bias in herself.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
Dhruv, you're mocking the new boy's English? Let your Payal Dadi tell you about a girl named Kamala.
I was sixteen, at a convent school in Allahabad. English was everything there. The girls who spoke it smoothly were made monitors and sent to welcome guests. Kamala came from a Hindi-medium school. When she read aloud, the nuns corrected every word, and we giggled.
I giggled too. Then we had a Hindi poetry recitation, and Kamala recited Mahadevi Verma so beautifully that the whole hall went silent. Afterwards I heard one of the nuns say, "Pity her English is so weak."
That sentence stayed with me. I thought: she's cleverer than all of us, and they only hear her accent. I started sitting with Kamala at lunch. She taught me Hindi poetry; I helped with her English.
So, Dhruv, the language someone speaks is not the size of their mind.

qa.q: Whose poetry did Kamala recite?
qa.a: Kamala recited Mahadevi Verma.

qa.q: How did Payal feel when she heard the nun's remark?
qa.a: Payal felt uncomfortable and troubled, realising that Kamala was cleverer than all of them but was judged only by her accent.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Payal's story?
qa.a: Hearing the nun say "Pity her English is so weak" after Kamala's recitation made Payal see the bias, and she began sitting with Kamala at lunch.

qa.q: What might Kamala have felt when the girls giggled at her reading?
qa.a: Kamala probably felt embarrassed and lonely, treated as lesser in a school where English was everything.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing as a teenager that fluent English earned respect while a Hindi-medium classmate was undervalued, and choosing to resist that bias.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
The inter-school quiz had thirty seconds per question, and the quizmaster only accepted answers in English. Abhinav, sixteen, sat at the buzzer beside his teammate Rafiq, who'd grown up speaking Urdu at home.
"Which river is called the Sorrow of Bihar?"
Rafiq whispered, "Kosi!" but then fumbled the English sentence. The buzzer on the other team went, and they got the points.
In the break, a boy from the other school laughed. "Your partner can't even speak English."
Abhinav felt his face go hot. He'd laughed at jokes like that before. Not now.
"He knew every answer in this round," Abhinav said. "Knowing and speaking English aren't the same thing."
He turned to Rafiq. "You answer, I'll say it in English. Just tell me fast."
For the next round, Rafiq whispered answers and Abhinav spoke them. They won by ten points.

qa.q: How many seconds did each question get?
qa.a: The inter-school quiz had thirty seconds per question.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when the boy laughed at Rafiq?
qa.a: Abhinav felt angry and a little ashamed, remembering that he had laughed at jokes like that before.

qa.q: What did Abhinav's plan show about language and intelligence?
qa.a: By letting Rafiq supply the answers while he spoke them in English, Abhinav showed that Rafiq's knowledge was never the problem, only the language rule.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel after they win?
qa.a: Rafiq would likely feel proud and relieved, his knowledge finally counted rather than judged by his English.

grounding: Under quiz pressure, a teenager notices that English fluency is mistaken for intelligence and resists the bias by standing with his teammate.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: In Class 10B of a Bengaluru school, the teacher asked who could explain photosynthesis. Jomon's hand went up first. He explained it perfectly, with a few Malayalam-flavoured vowels, and someone near the window said, "Say it in English, bro." Laughter. Then Rhea gave the same answer in a polished accent, and Mrs. Iyer said, "Excellent, very well spoken." Seema watched Jomon's ears go pink. She thought of her own mother, who read Kannada novels faster than anyone Seema knew but went silent at parent meetings. At lunch Seema sat beside Jomon. "Your answer had the chlorophyll part. Hers didn't." He looked up. "Really?" "Really. I checked the book." That evening Seema caught herself mocking a vegetable seller's English on the phone to a friend, and stopped mid-sentence.

qa.q: Which part did Seema say Jomon's answer had and Rhea's did not?
qa.a: Seema said Jomon's answer had the chlorophyll part.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling as she watched Jomon's ears go pink?
qa.a: Seema felt uneasy and sympathetic, recognising the same unfairness her mother faces at parent meetings.

qa.q: What could Mrs. Iyer have done differently?
qa.a: She could have praised Jomon's correct content first and stopped the "say it in English" laughter, showing that an accent says nothing about intelligence.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when the class laughed?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and hurt that a correct answer was mocked just for his vowels, which is why his ears went pink.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager noticing that polished English earns praise while a regional accent is mocked, and resisting that bias in others and in herself.
